questions.prompt: Iris, Cal, and Mara are in the kitchen. Mara just dropped a plate. Iris says, "It's fine — we have lots of plates." Cal says nothing. Whose silence carries the strongest subtext?

options.label: Cal's silence — it's louder than Iris's reassurance because Cal usually fills the room.
Iris's silence — wait, she just spoke.
Mara's silence — but she dropped the plate, so her quiet is expected.

questions.mentorPostScript: When a usually-talkative character goes quiet, the silence does more work than the line.

questions.prompt: Two listeners hear the same line: "You don't have to come if you don't want to." One is the person it's directed at; the other is overhearing. Why might the two hear different subtexts?

options.label: Because each listener brings their own history with the speaker — and history changes what a line means.
Because subtext is decided by a coin flip at the end of every scene.
Because only the speaker knows the subtext; listeners don't get one.

questions.mentorPostScript: The same line can carry two truths at once. Triangle scenes lean into this.

questions.prompt: Cal tells Iris, "I trust Mara." Mara is standing right there. Which is the strongest move for the subtext?

options.label: Mara doesn't react — she keeps doing what she was doing, and the steady action becomes the subtext.
Mara walks out of the scene.

questions.mentorPostScript: A character who DOESN'T react to a loaded line creates a kind of pressure the reader can feel.

questions.prompt: A line of dialogue can be honest on the surface AND honest underneath, BUT the two honesties say different things. Pick the line where this is true.

options.label: Iris: "I had a good day." (Her shoulders are tight; she's looking at the door.)
Cal: "WATCH OUT!" (A baseball is flying at Mara's head.)

questions.mentorPostScript: Two layers. The line tells the truth; the body tells a different truth. The reader holds both.

questions.prompt: In a triangle scene, Cal asks Iris a question that's really aimed at Mara. Which detail in the writing makes this clear?

options.label: Cal glances at Mara just before he speaks, then keeps his eyes on Iris while he asks the question.
Cal walks out of the room before asking anything.

questions.mentorPostScript: The glance is the redirect. The reader sees who the question is really for.
